title: Marasimha's Last Fast
subtitle: A feudatory king between sword and silence
era: Marasimha II's reign and death, c. 963-975 CE
moral: Power and renunciation can meet in one life.

sources.citation: Shravanabelagola and Bankapura inscriptions connected with Marasimha II and Jain ritual death
sources.note: Primary evidence for his piety and end-of-life tradition.

sources.citation: Rashtrakuta records of Krishna III and Khottiga's era mentioning Ganga feudatory service
S. Settar, Inviting Death (1989); B.A. Saletore, Medieval Jainism (1938)
sources.note: Source-critical treatment of sallekhana, Jain patronage and medieval Karnataka elites.

panels.shot: dramatic split-scene wide, half battlefield and half ascetic hall, seen from a slight low angle

dialogue.text: He won wars for emperors, then laid down his life grain by grain: the Ganga king Marasimha II, and the last fast at Bankapura.

panels.shot: broad aerial view sweeping over the Deccan plateau

dialogue.text: In the tenth century, the Deccan was a web of powers: Rashtrakuta emperors at Manyakheta, and their Ganga feudatories guarding Gangavadi in the south.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a palace hall with carved pillars

dialogue.text: Marasimha, styled Satyavakya, rose in this world as a Ganga prince of Gangavadi, sworn to serve the Rashtrakuta throne yet guarding his own line’s honor.

panels.shot: dynamic battlefield wide shot from behind Marasimha, overlooking troops

dialogue.text: In the reign of Krishna III and later Khottiga, inscriptions remember him in the field, leading Ganga forces for imperial campaigns while holding Gangavadi as a loyal yet forceful feudatory.

panels.shot: close shot of Marasimha on horseback at dusk

dialogue.text: The same records that praise his campaigns place him in a different light too, as a patron moving among Jain monks and mathas, his name etched later at Shravanabelagola and Bankapura.

panels.shot: intimate interior medium shot inside a Jain basadi

dialogue.speaker: marasimha_ii
dialogue.text: Guru, I have raised forts and burned camps. How does a king unlearn the sword?

panels.shot: slow push-in close-up on Marasimha's face lit by oil lamps

dialogue.text: By the 960s, his world tightened. The Rashtrakuta empire itself was fraying; feudatories like him bore both the weight of imperial wars and their own house’s fate.

panels.shot: wide shot of a fortified town identified through architecture as Bankapura

dialogue.text: Among the forts tied to his name was Bankapura in today’s Karnataka, later remembered in inscriptions as the place of his final vow.

panels.shot: medium shot in a palace chamber with attendants, from a slightly high angle

dialogue.text: At some point near the end of his career, the king laid these burdens down. The Bankapura record speaks of Marasimha undertaking sallekhana, the Jain fast unto death, under monastic guidance.

panels.shot: solemn interior wide shot of a Jain hall prepared for vows

dialogue.text: Sallekhana, described in Jain texts and studied by modern scholars, was a gradual, vowed thinning of the body, meant as a conscious exit, not a sudden flight from grief or defeat.

panels.shot: closer side-view of the vow-taking moment

dialogue.speaker: marasimha_ii
dialogue.text: As I leave each grain, may I leave each bond of anger and pride.

panels.shot: montage-style medium shot showing subtle progression over time

dialogue.text: The fast unfolded step by measured step. Food reduced, then water, as discipline and weakness wrestled in a body once trained for war.

panels.shot: gentle close-up on Marasimha's hand and face

dialogue.text: Inscriptions from Shravanabelagola to Bankapura praise such deaths as heroic restraint, though the wider world, even then, may not always have agreed in silence.

panels.shot: low, reverent shot from the feet of the seated king, looking up past him to the monk

dialogue.text: Modern debates ask whether such fasts can ever be wholly free, or wholly gentle, yet the stone records at Bankapura speak from the side of those who honored his choice.

panels.shot: close, detailed shot of a stone inscription surface

dialogue.text: Their language is formal and spare: it names the king, notes his vow, locates it at Bankapura, and folds his passing into a lineage of Jain patrons and warrior-ascetics.

panels.shot: soft wide shot showing the final moment in serene abstraction

dialogue.text: So ends the trace in stone: the king of Gangavadi, who once rode for Rashtrakutas, is last seen not in battle, but in a hall of silence at Bankapura.

panels.shot: modern-day wide shot of Shravanabelagola hill from a distance

dialogue.text: Today, at Shravanabelagola and other sites, historians read such epigraphs alongside Jain texts, weighing praise against pain, devotion against power, in trying to understand lives like Marasimha’s.

panels.shot: reflective medium-wide shot of an empty throne and a bare stone platform side by side

dialogue.text: His story endures as a hard question rather than an easy lesson: how a single life in medieval Karnataka could hold both the sword of a Rashtrakuta general and the slow, deliberate renunciation of sallekhana.
